findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The SQL query is built with an f-string that directly interpolates owner_id into the query text instead of using a parameterized query. If owner_id originates from user input (e.g., an authenticated caller's ID from a request), an attacker who can influence this value can inject arbitrary SQL, bypassing the intended WHERE clause and potentially reading or modifying other customers' data.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies an owner_id such as `' OR '1'='1` (or a more elaborate payload), which is concatenated verbatim into the SQL string, allowing the query to return or affect rows belonging to other customers, leading to unauthorized data disclosure or manipulation.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
    return [dict(row) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
findings.title: Fix SQL injection in load_order_rows via f-string query

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: `events: list[str] = []` creates the default list once at function-definition time, and it is shared and mutated (`events.append(...)`) across every call that omits the argument. Each call permanently grows this shared list, so it never shrinks and accumulates every event type ever passed in across the process lifetime.
findings.failure_scenario: When the function is called repeatedly without an explicit `events` argument (e.g. in a request-handling loop), the shared default list keeps growing on every call, leaking memory and causing the returned event list to include stale entries from unrelated prior calls.
findings.title: Replace the mutable default list argument with None

findings.body: The loop iterates `range(1, len(entries))`, which skips `entries[0]` entirely. That entry is never scored and never appears in the returned ranked list, even if it has the highest score.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling rank_invoice_entries on any list drops the first element from scoring, so a top-scoring entry that happens to be first in the input list is silently omitted from the ranked output.
findings.suggestion: for position in range(len(entries)):
findings.title: Start ranking from index 0 to include the first entry

findings.body: The function accepts a `threshold: float` parameter but never uses it — it hardcodes the comparison against `5000` instead. Callers passing a custom threshold get silently ignored behavior, which is a functional bug introduced by this change.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes `flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, threshold=1000)` expecting rows above 1000 to be flagged, but the function still only flags rows above the hardcoded 5000, so rows between 1000 and 5000 are missed from review flagging.
findings.suggestion: if float(row["total"]) > threshold:
findings.title: flag_large_backorder_totals ignores its threshold parameter

findings.body: `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` returns a naive datetime with no timezone information, and it is deprecated in recent Python versions in favor of timezone-aware alternatives. Stamping manifest checkpoints with a naive UTC timestamp can create ambiguity when these timestamps are compared with timezone-aware values elsewhere in the system.
findings.failure_scenario: Checkpoints stamped with a naive datetime get compared or serialized alongside timezone-aware timestamps from other parts of the pipeline, causing incorrect ordering or comparison errors (`TypeError: can't compare naive and aware datetimes`), and on newer Python runtimes this call path also emits deprecation warnings ahead of removal.
findings.title: Use a timezone-aware timestamp instead of naive utcnow()

findings.body: The innermost condition `weight > 0 and zone` does not reference `carrier` at all, so every carrier in `carriers` receives the exact same count (len(zones) * len(weights), filtered by truthy checks that don't depend on carrier). The function name and docstring claim per-carrier counting, but the carrier-specific logic appears to be missing.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling cross_check_tariff_routes with distinct carriers expecting carrier-specific viable route counts returns identical values for every carrier, masking real differences in routing feasibility between carriers.
findings.title: Viable route count never varies per carrier

findings.body: unique_payment_labels dedupes by checking `label in seen` against a growing list for every row, which is O(n^2) overall. dict.fromkeys() preserves first-seen order in O(n) and removes the need for the separate `seen` accumulator entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: On large row lists, the repeated linear `label in seen` scans make deduplication quadratic, so runtime grows much faster than necessary as the number of rows increases.
findings.title: Use dict.fromkeys() instead of a manual dedup loop

findings.anchor: def newest_queue_id(records: list[dict[str, object]]) -> str | None:
findings.body: The docstring says this returns the newest id 'in constant time' and explicitly assumes chronological order, yet the body still sorts the entire records list before taking the last element. Given the stated assumption, the sort is pure wasted work — the last element can be read directly.
findings.failure_scenario: When records is large, sorting the whole list on every call costs O(n log n) despite the docstring's promise of constant time, adding unnecessary CPU overhead that scales with input size for callers relying on the documented performance characteristic.
findings.title: Drop the unnecessary sort in newest_queue_id

findings.body: The docstring states the function returns the newest queue identifier 'in constant time' and 'assumes records arrive in chronological order,' yet the implementation still calls `sorted(records, ...)`, which is O(n log n) and ignores the stated chronological-order assumption entirely. Either the docstring is wrong or the implementation fails to exploit the assumption it documents.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers relying on the documented O(1) behavior for large record sets will see unexpected latency from the full sort on every call, and the redundant sort also means the 'assumes chronological order' precondition is never actually leveraged, making the contract misleading.
findings.title: newest_queue_id docstring claims constant time but implementation sorts

findings.body: `seen` is a list, and the membership check `label in seen` is O(n) per row, making the whole function O(n²) as the number of rows grows. A set gives O(1) membership checks and preserves the same first-seen ordering via the separate `labels` list.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` contains many entries with few duplicates, each iteration re-scans the growing `seen` list linearly, so processing time grows quadratically with the row count and becomes a bottleneck for large payment batches.
findings.suggestion: seen: set[str] = set()
findings.title: Use a set for duplicate tracking instead of a list

findings.body: The inner double loop over `zones` and `weights` computes `count` the same way for every carrier because the condition `weight > 0 and zone` never references `carrier`. Recomputing this identical O(zones × weights) scan once per carrier wastes work proportional to `len(carriers)` for no behavioral benefit.
findings.failure_scenario: When `carriers` has many entries, the nested zone/weight scan (already O(zones × weights)) is repeated once per carrier instead of once total, so total work scales as O(carriers × zones × weights) instead of O(zones × weights + carriers), slowing down calls with large carrier lists.
findings.title: Hoist the carrier-independent count out of the carrier loop

findings.body: The inner double loop just counts zone/weight pairs that satisfy independent conditions (zone truthy, weight > 0), and it repeats that O(zones × weights) scan once per carrier even though the result never depends on which carrier is being processed. The nested loops obscure the fact that this is a simple product of two independent counts, making the function harder to read and needlessly quadratic-per-carrier.
findings.suggestion:
valid_zones = sum(1 for zone in zones if zone)
        valid_weights = sum(1 for weight in weights if weight > 0)
        viable[carrier] = valid_zones * valid_weights
findings.title: Simplify the triple-nested loop counting viable routes

findings.body: `events: list[str] = []` uses a mutable default argument, which is created once at function-definition time and shared across every call that omits `events`. Each call appends to the same shared list instead of starting fresh, so state leaks between unrelated calls.
findings.failure_scenario: Two separate calls to `register_shipment_events('created')` and later `register_shipment_events('shipped')` without passing `events` will both mutate the same underlying list, so the second call's returned event list unexpectedly includes 'created' from the prior call, corrupting the per-type event history.
findings.title: Avoid mutable default argument in register_shipment_events

findings.anchor: def rank_invoice_entries(entries: list[dict[str, object]]) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
findings.body: rank_invoice_entries builds a scored list by hand and calls .sort() with a key, which is exactly what sorted(entries, key=..., reverse=True) already does in one line. Worse, the hand-rolled loop iterates with range(1, len(entries)), which starts at index 1 instead of 0 and silently drops the first entry from the ranking — a direct consequence of reimplementing iteration logic instead of using the stdlib primitive.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling rank_invoice_entries on any non-empty list skips entries[0] because the loop starts at index 1, so the top-ranked or lowest-ranked entry (depending on data) never appears in the returned ranking.
findings.title: Collapse the manual score-and-sort loop into sorted()

findings.failure_scenario: With a large number of carriers and a sizeable zones/weights matrix, the same zone/weight scan is redundantly repeated once per carrier, multiplying the cost by the carrier count and slowing down callers that pass realistic route/carrier volumes.
findings.title: Hoist the route-viability count out of the carrier loop

findings.failure_scenario: A caller relies on the docstring's "constant time" claim and invokes newest_queue_id repeatedly inside a hot loop over growing record sets, expecting O(1) cost per call; instead each call performs a full sort, turning what the caller believes is linear overall work into quadratic time and causing unexpected latency at scale.
